opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are several vectors of progress, and people sometimes focus too narrowly on just one of them.

The first is the one everyone talks about: scaling. Bigger models, more data, more compute. That's still driving progress, though I think we're seeing that it's getting harder and more expensive to squeeze out each increment that way. It's not over, but it's no longer the only game in town.

The second, which I'm really excited about, is agentic workflows. Today a lot of people still use large language models in a zero-shot way, as if you asked someone to write an essay from start to finish without ever hitting backspace. And it's amazing they do as well as they do! But when you let the model iterate, so it writes a draft, critiques it, does some research, uses tools, revises, and maybe splits the work across multiple agents, you often get dramatically better results. On a lot of coding benchmarks, for example, wrapping an older model in a good agentic workflow can outperform a newer model used zero-shot. So much of the near-term improvement in what AI can actually do for people will come from these workflow design patterns: reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent collaboration.

Third, there's a lot of progress coming from the data side, what I've long called data-centric AI. Carefully engineering the data you train or fine-tune on, including synthetic data and reasoning traces, turns out to be enormously powerful, and it's often underrated relative to architecture or scale.

Fourth, and this is less glamorous, inference is getting faster and cheaper. Token prices have been falling rapidly. That matters because agentic workflows consume a lot of tokens. When the model can "think" much more for the same cost, you can afford to have it reflect, retry, and explore, and that translates directly into capability.

And then there's multimodality. We're still early in what visual AI and these large vision models can do, and I think a lot of value will come from AI that can understand images, video, and the physical world, not just text.

So my view is that capabilities will keep improving steadily, but not from one single breakthrough. It'll come from many teams pushing on all of these fronts at once. And honestly, for most builders, the bottleneck today isn't the frontier capability of the models. It's that we haven't yet figured out how to build all the applications that the current models already make possible. There's a huge amount of value just waiting to be built.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling is still driving progress but is getting harder and more expensive for each increment.

r002.rationale: It says people focus narrowly on scaling, but does not attribute that emphasis to PR influence or a handful of companies.

r003.rationale: It identifies agentic workflows, including iteration, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration, as a source of improvement.

r004.rationale: It does not raise using diffusion models to generate text.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, I think there's a tendency to treat "AI capabilities" as one thing that goes up or down, and I find it more useful to break it apart, because the different pieces are moving at really different speeds.

The first piece is the raw models themselves. Scaling has worked remarkably well, and I don't think it's done. But I do think the easy gains from just making the model bigger and training on more of the internet are getting harder to find. We're running out of high-quality human-written text, compute is expensive, and the leading labs are increasingly turning to things like synthetic data, reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks, and smarter post-training. So I expect continued progress there, but more of it will come from cleverness than from brute force.

The second piece, and honestly the one I'm most excited about, is what you can build on top of these models. Agentic workflows, where instead of asking a model to write an essay in one shot you have it plan, draft, critique its own work, use tools, go search for something, and iterate, give you a huge jump in results, even with today's models. I've seen cases where an older model wrapped in a good agentic workflow outperforms a newer, bigger model used naively. That means a lot of the capability improvement over the next few years won't require any new breakthrough in the underlying model at all. It's engineering, and it's available to anyone willing to do the work.

The third piece is cost. Token prices have been falling incredibly fast, and that changes what's economically feasible. Things that were technically possible but too expensive, like running a model over millions of documents, or having an agent take dozens of steps to finish one task, suddenly become reasonable. Cheaper intelligence is a capability improvement in its own right, even if the benchmark score doesn't move.

And then there's a fourth thing, which I'd call the tooling and the know-how. Evals, observability, prompt and data engineering, the whole discipline of actually making this stuff work reliably in production. That's maturing, and it's what lets a small team ship something that works instead of a flashy demo that falls over.

So if you ask me where it goes from here, I'd say the models keep getting better, somewhat more slowly than the last couple of years, but the usable capability, what a developer can actually deploy, keeps improving quite fast because all these other layers are compounding. I'm less worried about whether AI keeps improving and more focused on the fact that there's already a massive gap between what the technology can do and what's been built with it. Closing that gap is where most of the value is, and it's also where I'd encourage most people to spend their time.

r001.rationale: The response says easy gains from making models bigger and training on more internet data are getting harder to find.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute public emphasis on scaling to PR influence by a handful of companies.

r003.rationale: It describes agentic workflows—planning, using tools, and iterating—as a way to improve results even with current models.

r004.rationale: It mentions synthetic data but does not raise using diffusion models to generate text.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will continue to improve along several dimensions. Scaling up models is one of them, but I wouldn’t look only at the next generation of foundation models. There’s also a lot of progress to be made in how we build systems around them.

For example, if you ask a model to solve a difficult problem in one shot, it may struggle. But if you let it break the problem into steps, use tools, check its work, and revise its answer, you can get much better results. So even with a fixed model, better workflows can unlock additional capabilities.

And then there’s the question of cost. When intelligence becomes cheaper and faster, developers can afford to experiment more and apply it to problems that previously weren’t economical. That can have a very large impact even when it doesn’t show up as a dramatic jump on a benchmark.

So I’m optimistic. Better models, better workflows, and lower costs all reinforce one another. The challenge is turning those capabilities into reliable applications that actually help people.

r001.rationale: The response mentions scaling up models but does not say that further progress through scaling is becoming more difficult.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute public emphasis on scaling to PR influence by a handful of companies.

r003.rationale: It describes systems breaking problems into steps, using tools, checking work, and revising as a way to improve results beyond scaling models.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention diffusion models or generating text with them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think progress will come from several directions. Better models are one, and I expect that to continue. But a lot of the practical gains will also come from how we build systems around those models.

For example, instead of asking a model to produce a perfect answer in one shot, you can let it draft an answer, check its work, use tools, and revise. Those workflows give us another way to improve performance, even without changing the underlying model.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t think of capabilities as a single number going up. Different tasks will improve at different rates. The useful question is: for a particular task, can we build a system that performs reliably enough to create value? I think the range of tasks where the answer is yes will keep expanding.
